title: The King Enters, the Temple Judged, a Fig Tree Withers
summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt while crowds shout Hosanna and bless the coming kingdom of David. The next day he curses a leafy fig tree without fruit, drives the traders from the temple courts, and quotes the prophets against the temple's keepers. When the disciples see the fig tree withered, he teaches them about faith, prayer, and forgiveness, and when the temple authorities challenge his authority he answers with a question about John the Baptist that they refuse to answer.
story:
The road that began at Caesarea Philippi (8:27) ends here. Everything from this chapter to the end of Mark happens in and around Jerusalem in about a week, and Mark marks the days: the arrival (verse 11), ‘the next day’ (verse 12), and ‘in the morning’ (verse 20). The last six chapters of the Gospel, more than a third of the book, tell of these few days.

Jesus arrives as the Son of David whom Bartimaeus hailed at Jericho, and he stages his arrival as a deliberate sign, sending for a colt and riding into the city among pilgrims who sing the psalms of the feast. But his first act in the city is quiet: he enters the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves (verse 11). The next day he returns and acts, overturning the tables of the traders and declaring that God's house has become a den of robbers. The confrontation with the temple leadership that fills chapters 11 and 12 begins here, and verse 18 states its outcome in advance: the chief priests and scribes look for a way to destroy him. From now on the opposition is led not by Galilean Pharisees but by the priestly rulers of Jerusalem, the men Jesus named in his first passion prediction (8:31). The chapter ends with their question, ‘By what authority?’, which the rest of the Gospel answers.
historical:
Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, the ridge that rises across the Kidron Valley from the temple mount. Bethany lay about 3 kilometers (under 2 miles) from the city (John 11:18 gives fifteen stadia), and Jesus lodged there during the week (verse 11, 14:3). The Mount of Olives carried prophetic weight: Zechariah 14:4 pictures the LORD's feet standing on it on the day he comes to judge and save. Josephus tells of an Egyptian prophet in the 50s who led a crowd to the Mount of Olives promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.169-172), which shows how the place could stir hopes of deliverance.

Passover crowds swelled Jerusalem many times over. Josephus reports a count of Passover lambs taken under the governor Cestius Gallus in the 60s, 256,500, and from it calculates a crowd of more than two and a half million (Jewish War 6.422-427); the figures are surely inflated, but they show the scale of the feast. Roman governors came up from Caesarea at the festivals with troops, because crowds celebrating Israel's liberation from Egypt could turn against Rome, and the Antonia fortress overlooked the temple courts (Acts 21:31-35).

The temple Jesus entered was Herod the Great's rebuilding of the second temple, begun in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20 or 19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.380), and still being finished in Jesus' day (John 2:20). Herod doubled the platform to about 14 hectares (35 acres), one of the largest sacred precincts in the Roman world. Along its southern side he built the Royal Stoa, a vast colonnaded hall (Antiquities 15.411-416), probably where much of the court's business took place. The outer court was open to Gentiles; a stone balustrade marked the point beyond which foreigners could not go, and one of its Greek warning inscriptions, threatening death to any foreigner who passed, was found in 1871 (compare Josephus, Jewish War 5.193-194).

The trade Jesus disrupted served real needs. Pilgrims needed unblemished animals and birds for sacrifice, and every Jewish man owed a yearly half-shekel for the temple (Exodus 30:13). The Mishnah says money changers set up tables in the temple on the twenty-fifth of Adar, about three weeks before Passover (m. Shekalim 1:3), and rabbinic rules fixed the temple's payments to the Tyrian standard (m. Bekhorot 8:7), since the silver coins of Tyre were reliably pure, despite the image of the god Melqart on them. Doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7, 12:8), and the Mishnah records that Rabbi Simeon ben Gamaliel forced down the price of a pair of doves when it had risen to a gold denar (m. Keritot 1:7). The temple was run by the high priest, in these years Joseph Caiaphas (about AD 18 to 36), son-in-law of Annas, whose family dominated the office. The Babylonian Talmud preserves a lament over the high priestly houses of Boethus, Annas (Hanin), Kathros, and Ishmael ben Phiabi, for their clubs, whisperings, pens, and fists (b. Pesachim 57a), a later Jewish memory of a wealthy and violent priestly aristocracy. Victor Eppstein (1964) argued that Caiaphas had recently moved the animal trade onto the temple mount itself; the proposal is possible but unproven.

Jesus was not the only Jew to speak against the temple. Jeremiah had done so in the temple gate (Jeremiah 7, 26), the Qumran community rejected the Jerusalem priesthood as corrupt, and Josephus tells of another Jesus, son of Ananias, who from AD 62 cried woe against Jerusalem and the temple at the feasts, was handed over by the Jewish leaders to the governor Albinus, flogged, and released as a madman (Jewish War 6.300-309).
cultural:
A colt ‘on which no one has ever sat’ (verse 2) was fit for a sacred purpose; the law set apart animals never yoked for holy use (Numbers 19:2, Deuteronomy 21:3, 1 Samuel 6:7). Kings in Israel rode mules and donkeys on solemn occasions: David had Solomon ride his own mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33-40). Zechariah 9:9 pictures Zion's king coming humble, riding on a donkey's colt, and the next verse says he will cut off the war horse and speak peace to the nations. Mark does not quote Zechariah, as Matthew and John do, but readers who knew the prophet would hear it. Borrowing an animal with the words ‘The Lord needs it’ echoes the right of kings and officials to requisition transport, though Jesus promises to send it back.

Spreading garments on the road was a royal welcome (2 Kings 9:13, when Jehu was proclaimed king), and branches were carried at national celebrations: when Simon the Maccabee took the citadel of Jerusalem in 141 BC, the people entered with praise and palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51), and branches were carried at the rededication of the temple (2 Maccabees 10:7). The crowd's cries come from Psalm 118, the last of the Hallel psalms (113 to 118) sung at the great feasts. Hosanna transliterates the Hebrew hoshi'ah na, ‘save, please’ (Psalm 118:25), which by Jesus' time had become a shout of praise as well as a plea. ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord’ was the priests' blessing on pilgrims arriving at the temple (Psalm 118:26). The crowd adds a line of its own, “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!”, revealing a hope for the restoration of David's kingdom, a hope the Psalms of Solomon (17:21-32) had prayed for a century earlier.

Fig trees were among the chief trees of the land, and sitting under one's own vine and fig tree was a picture of peace (Micah 4:4). In the hill country near Jerusalem they put out leaves in spring, around Passover, together with small unripe knobs (Hebrew paggim) that were sometimes eaten; the first ripe figs came in early summer and the main crop in late summer. Mark's note that ‘it was not the season for figs’ (verse 13) tells the reader that the act is a sign, not a gardener's judgment. The prophets had used the fig tree and its fruit as pictures of Israel before God (Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10 and 16, Micah 7:1), and the fruitless tree as a picture of judgment.

The temple mount was a sacred space with its own rules. The Mishnah forbids entering it with a staff, sandals, a money belt, or dust on one's feet, and forbids using it as a shortcut (m. Berakhot 9:5), which may explain Jesus' refusal to let anyone carry goods through the courts (verse 16). Debating by answering a question with a question was a recognized form of argument among Jewish teachers. Prayer was commonly offered standing (1 Samuel 1:26, 1 Kings 8:22, Luke 18:11-13), and the synagogue's central prayer came to be called the Amidah, ‘the standing’, which is why verse 25 speaks of standing to pray. To say something came ‘from heaven’ (verse 30) was a reverent way of saying ‘from God’, as in Daniel 4:26.
literary:
Mark frames the temple action with the fig tree, one of his characteristic sandwiches (compare 3:20-35, 5:21-43, 6:7-30): the curse (verses 12 to 14), the temple (15 to 19), and the withered tree (20 to 21). Each half interprets the other. The tree is all leaves and no fruit, and so, in Jesus' judgment, is the temple system: busy, impressive, and barren of what God sought. Matthew tells the same events in a different order, with the temple action on the day of the entry and the fig tree withering at once (Matthew 21:12-20); Mark's arrangement makes the tree a frame around the temple.

The chapter moves in three days. Day one is the entry and the silent inspection (1 to 11). Day two is the curse and the temple action (12 to 19). Day three opens with the withered tree and teaching on faith (20 to 25) and continues with the challenge to Jesus' authority (27 to 33), which leads without a break into the parable and debates of chapter 12. The entry is told with the same pattern of command and fulfillment Mark will use for the preparation of the Passover (14:12-16): Jesus sends two disciples, tells them what they will find and what to say, and it happens ‘as Jesus had instructed them’.

The chapter's Scripture is woven rather than cited. Psalm 118 supplies the crowd's words and will return in 12:10-11, where its rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. Zechariah stands behind the colt, the Mount of Olives, and possibly the removal of traders from the LORD's house (Zechariah 9:9, 14:4, 14:21). Jesus explains his action with two explicit quotations. Mark alone keeps the full wording of Isaiah 56:7, “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations”, which highlights that the court where Gentiles could pray had become a market. The second phrase, “a den of robbers”, comes from Jeremiah 7:11, where Jeremiah stood in the temple gate and warned that the building would not protect a people who did injustice, and that God would do to it what he had done to Shiloh.

The debate that closes the chapter follows the form of a controversy story: a hostile question, a counter-question, and the questioners silenced. Mark lets the reader overhear the leaders' private reasoning (verses 31 and 32), and he breaks off their sentence in the middle, finishing it as narrator (they ‘were afraid of the people’). Their answer, ‘We do not know’, is not ignorance but a refusal to decide, and Jesus' refusal to answer them mirrors it.

outline.t: Jesus curses the fruitless fig tree
The withered fig tree: faith, prayer, and forgiveness

doctrines.note: Jesus enters the temple as one with authority over it, inspects it, and judges it by its own purpose: a house of prayer for all the nations. The fig tree that withers from the roots signals that the institution in its present form will not stand, and the chapter points toward a new center of God's presence, which the Gospel will locate in Jesus himself (14:58, 15:38).

The fig tree and the temple action together are a prophetic sign of judgment on a religious center that looked flourishing but bore no fruit. Jesus stands in the line of Jeremiah, who warned that God would not spare a temple whose worshipers trusted the building and ignored justice (Jeremiah 7:1-15).

The entry is a deliberate royal act. Jesus arranges it, receives the crowd's acclamation of David's coming kingdom, and enters the temple as its Lord. Yet he comes on a colt, not a war horse, as Zechariah's humble king, and the kingdom he brings will be established through his death.

Jesus holds the temple to its calling as a house of prayer and then teaches his disciples to pray with faith in God and to forgive when they pray (verses 22 to 25). As the temple's role is called into question, the chapter points to a people whose prayer rests on God himself, not on a building, and whose prayer cannot coexist with a grudge.

‘Have faith in God’ (verse 22) grounds the saying about the mountain in God, not in the strength of the believer's certainty. Faith here is trust that God can do what is humanly impossible, joined in the same breath to forgiveness of others; it is not a technique for obtaining what one wants.

words.note: Hōsanna, a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew hoshi'ah na, ‘save, please’, from Psalm 118:25. It occurs six times in the New Testament, only in the entry scenes (Matthew 21:9 and 15, Mark 11:9 and 10, John 12:13). The Greek Old Testament translated the phrase (sōson dē) rather than transliterating it. By Jesus' time the plea had become a shout of praise at the feasts, and it passed into Christian worship in the Sanctus of the eucharistic prayer and the Didache's eucharistic prayers (Didache 10:6).

Pōlos, colt, the young of an animal. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, all in the entry stories, four times in this chapter. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew for a young donkey (Genesis 49:11, Zechariah 9:9). Walter Bauer argued that the word used alone meant a young horse, but most scholars reply that here, as Matthew and John make explicit, it means a donkey's colt.

Sukē, fig tree. It occurs about fifteen times in the New Testament, three times in this chapter and once more in the parable of 13:28. Figs were one of the seven species of the land (Deuteronomy 8:8), and a fig tree bearing fruit pictured peace and blessing (Micah 4:4). A leafy, fruitless fig tree made a pointed sign, and the prophets had used the same image for an Israel that gave God nothing (Jeremiah 8:13).

Hieron, temple, the whole sacred precinct with its courts, as distinct from naos, the sanctuary building itself. It occurs about seventy times in the New Testament and nine times in Mark, five in this chapter. Mark uses hieron for the place Jesus inspects, clears, and teaches in, and naos when the sanctuary is threatened or its curtain torn (14:58, 15:29, 15:38).

Lēstēs, robber or bandit. It occurs fifteen times in the New Testament and three times in Mark: here, at Jesus' arrest, when he protests that they have come for him as for a robber (14:48), and for the two men crucified with him (15:27). Josephus uses the word for violent insurgents. It comes into Jesus' words from Jeremiah 7:11, where a den of robbers is a hideout where thieves feel safe after their crimes.

Proseuchē, prayer. It occurs thirty-six times in the New Testament and twice in Mark (9:29 and here, verse 17), with the related verb proseuchomai in verses 24 and 25. Isaiah 56:7 promised that foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD would be brought to his holy mountain, and that his house would be a house of prayer for all peoples. Jesus holds the temple to that purpose and then teaches his disciples about prayer themselves.

Aphiēmi, to release, let go, and so to forgive. It occurs about 143 times in the New Testament with a wide range (leave, permit, forgive), and in this chapter it means to let go or permit (verses 6 and 16) and, twice in verse 25, to forgive. BDAG treats forgiving as releasing someone from a debt or obligation. Forgiveness here is the condition of honest prayer.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about 102 times in the New Testament and ten times in Mark, four in verses 28 to 33. The crowds noticed from the start that Jesus taught with authority unlike the scribes (1:22), and he claimed authority to forgive sins (2:10). The leaders' question (verse 28) asks both what kind of authority and who gave it, and the rest of Mark answers it.

christ:
Jesus enters Jerusalem as its king and the temple as its Lord. Mark shows him in command of every step: he knows where the colt is tied, what will be said, and what the owners will allow, and he calls himself, or God, ‘the Lord’ who needs it (verse 3). He rides in as Zechariah's king, righteous and humble, coming to speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:9-10), and the crowd greets him with the pilgrim blessing of Psalm 118 and the hope of David's kingdom. Mark does not say the crowd understood what kind of king this was, and within days a crowd will shout for his crucifixion (15:13-14).

The deeper claim concerns the temple. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom Israel sought would suddenly come to his temple, and that his coming would be a refining fire (Malachi 3:1-3). Mark opened his Gospel by quoting that verse about the messenger who prepares the Lord's way (1:2), and that is why Jesus answers the question about his authority by pointing to John the Baptist, the messenger. If John was from heaven, the one John prepared for is the Lord of the temple. Jesus looks around at everything in it (verse 11) the way the owner inspects his house, and the next day he judges it. The sign is not only a reform of abuses; the withered fig tree around it announces that the temple's time is ending. In Mark the charge at his trial will be that he said he would destroy the temple made with hands and build another not made with hands (14:58), the temple curtain will tear as he dies (15:38), and the house of prayer for all the nations will be gathered around the risen Christ, whom the New Testament calls the cornerstone of a new temple (1 Peter 2:4-7, Ephesians 2:19-22). John's Gospel makes the connection explicit: the temple he spoke of was his body (John 2:19-21).

The teaching on prayer shows the same shift. Faith is directed to God (verse 22), and prayer rests on the Father in heaven who forgives (verse 25), not on the sacrifices of the house Jesus has just judged. Jesus himself will pray on the Mount of Olives, in Gethsemane, asking that the cup pass and submitting to the Father's will (14:32-36), which is the pattern that governs every promise about prayer in this chapter.

Finally, the question ‘By what authority?’ is the question the whole Gospel answers. Jesus' authority comes from heaven: the voice at his baptism named him the beloved Son (1:11), and the parable that follows at once in 12:1-12 tells of an owner who sends his servants and then his beloved son to a vineyard. The leaders refuse to say whether John was from heaven, and so they cannot see who Jesus is. The king who comes humbly on a colt will be enthroned on a cross, and the temple he judges will be replaced by his own body raised on the third day.
interpretation:
The entry into Jerusalem shaped Christian worship early. The pilgrim Egeria, visiting Jerusalem in the early 380s, described the church's procession on the Sunday before Easter: the people gathered on the Mount of Olives, heard the Gospel of the entry read, and walked down into the city with branches, singing ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Itinerary 31). The Palm Sunday procession spread from Jerusalem across East and West. Theodulf of Orléans wrote the Palm Sunday hymn Gloria, laus et honor about 820, known in English through John Mason Neale's translation as All Glory, Laud and Honor, and in German lands medieval processions drew a wooden Christ on a donkey (the Palmesel) through the streets. The crowd's words entered the eucharistic liturgy: the Hosanna and the Benedictus follow the Sanctus in the Mass and in many Protestant orders of communion, and the Didache's table prayers already include ‘Hosanna to the God of David’ (Didache 10:6). In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, verses 1 to 11 are read at the Liturgy of the Palms, with John 12:12-16 as the alternative. Johann Sebastian Bach wrote his cantata Himmelskönig, sei willkommen (BWV 182) for Palm Sunday 1714. In art, Giotto painted both the Entry into Jerusalem and the Expulsion of the Money-changers in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (about 1303 to 1305), and El Greco painted Christ Driving the Traders from the Temple at least four times, from a version of about 1570 now in Washington to one of about 1600 in the National Gallery, London.

The fig tree troubled readers from the start. John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 67) explained that Jesus showed his power to punish on a tree rather than on people, as a mercy and a warning. Many patristic and medieval commentators read the tree as the synagogue, all leaves of observance and no fruit of faith, a reading that fed Christian contempt for Jews. Bertrand Russell, in Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), cited the story as evidence of a defect in Jesus' character, since, as Mark says, it was not the season for figs. Modern scholars, following William Telford (The Barren Temple and the Withered Tree, 1980), mostly read it as an acted prophecy tied to the temple, and they reject the step from the temple's leadership to the Jewish people.

The temple action has been read as a cleansing of abuses, as in the Reformation woodcuts of Lucas Cranach's Passional Christi und Antichristi (1521), which set Christ driving out the money changers opposite the pope selling indulgences. E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) argued that it was not a cleansing at all but a symbolic act announcing the temple's destruction and replacement in God's coming kingdom; Craig Evans (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1989) replied that Jewish sources show there was plenty to cleanse, and N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) read the action and the fig tree together as an enacted judgment. Paula Fredriksen has doubted that the scene happened as Mark describes it, arguing that it fits the Gospels' plot too neatly.

The promise about the mountain has had its own history. The Word of Faith teacher Kenneth Hagin made Mark 11:23-24 the center of his ministry, teaching that believers can have what they say in faith; most Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox teachers have rejected that reading, as the hard question below explains.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter. Its text is partly preserved in the third-century papyrus P45, which holds portions of Mark 11 and 12.

Verse 3: the critical text has Jesus promise that the Lord ‘will return it shortly’ (with palin, ‘back’); the Textus Receptus, followed by the King James Version, reads ‘straightway he will send him hither’, making the owner the one who sends the colt. Verse 8: the KJV's ‘and strawed them in the way’ comes from later manuscripts. Verse 10: the KJV adds ‘that cometh in the name of the Lord’ to the blessing on David's kingdom, from later manuscripts that repeated the line from verse 9. Verse 19: editions differ between ‘they went out’ and ‘he went out’.

Verse 22: a few early witnesses, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae, read ‘if you have faith in God’, making the verse a condition leading into verse 23; the critical editions print the command. Verse 24: the earliest manuscripts read ‘believe that you have received it’ (an aorist, elabete); later manuscripts read ‘you receive’ or ‘you will receive’, smoothing the unusual tense.

Verse 26: ‘But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses’ is absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Washingtonianus, and other early witnesses, and closely matches Matthew 6:15, from which it was probably added. The KJV and NKJV print it; modern critical editions and most modern English Bibles omit it or place it in a footnote, which is why the BSB and others skip from verse 25 to verse 27.

The Gospels also order the events differently. Matthew and Luke place the temple action on the day of the entry; John places a temple action at the beginning of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13-22). Some interpreters hold that there were two such events; others think John moved the one event to the front of his Gospel for theological reasons.

teach.big: Jesus comes to Jerusalem as its humble king and to the temple as its Lord, judging worship that bears no fruit and calling his people to a life of faith, prayer, and forgiveness that rests on God himself.

outline.t: Jesus is in command of his own entry: he sends for the colt, knows what will be found, and fulfills the picture of the humble king who comes in peace.
The crowd welcomes the king with the psalm of the pilgrims and its own hope for David's kingdom; Jesus goes straight to the temple and looks at everything, as its owner.
A tree full of leaves and empty of fruit becomes an acted sign: God looks for fruit, not display, and what bears none will not stand.
Jesus judges the temple by its own purpose, a house of prayer for all nations, and the leaders who profit from it decide he must be destroyed.
When the old center falls, faith rests on God himself: prayer can ask for the impossible, and prayer that asks for forgiveness must also give it.
Those who refuse to say where John's authority came from cannot see where Jesus' authority comes from; honest questions receive answers, evasions do not.

teach.pitfalls:
Palm Sunday is often preached as a celebration that turned sour, with the fickle crowd as the moral. Mark's point is more pointed: the king comes humbly, inspects God's house, and judges it, and the question is whether we welcome that kind of king. The temple action is commonly reduced to a rule against selling things in church buildings, or used to license anger as righteous; Jesus' act was a prophetic sign of judgment by the Lord of the temple, not a model for private outbursts.

The fig tree is misread in two directions: as a fit of temper that must be explained away, or as a sign against the Jewish people as a whole. Mark ties it to the temple leadership, not to Israel, and the crowd in this chapter hangs on Jesus' words (verse 18). Teachers should be careful not to repeat the old Christian reading that made the withered tree a picture of the synagogue.

Verses 23 and 24 are among the most misused verses in the Gospels, taught as a guarantee that confident faith obtains whatever one asks. The promise is framed by faith in God (verse 22) and followed at once by forgiveness (verse 25), and Jesus' own prayer in Gethsemane was not granted. Finally, the leaders' ‘We do not know’ is often taught as mere cowardice; it is also a warning about religious leadership that calculates answers by their consequences rather than by the truth.
teach.pastoral: The prayer promise in verses 22 to 25 presses on people who have prayed and not received what they asked: parents who prayed for a child's healing, people who prayed to be freed from depression or addiction, anyone told that their faith was too weak. Teach with care that Jesus does not make answered prayer depend on the strength of our certainty, and that he himself prayed for the cup to pass and was not spared (14:36). Unanswered prayer is not proof of weak faith. Verse 25 also presses on people who have been deeply wronged; forgiveness does not mean pretending harm did not happen, returning to danger, or giving up the pursuit of justice, and it may take time. It means releasing the debt to God rather than holding it as one's own weapon.

hard.q: Why would Jesus curse a fig tree for having no fruit when it was not the season for figs?
hard.a:
The objection is sharp and old. Mark himself says it was not the season for figs (verse 13), so the tree did nothing wrong, and Jesus destroys it because he is hungry and finds nothing. Bertrand Russell, in Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), named the story as one reason he could not regard Jesus as the best and wisest of men: it seemed petulant, and you could not blame the tree. Critical scholars add that the story looks like a parable turned into a miracle (Luke has a parable of a barren fig tree instead, Luke 13:6-9), and Jewish readers have objected that Christians used the withered tree for centuries as a picture of the Jewish people cursed and rejected, a reading that fed contempt and worse.

Responses begin with Mark's own framing. Mark places the curse and the withering around the temple action, and by saying it was not the season for figs he signals that the scene is not about horticulture but about a sign. The prophets had used the image of a fig tree without fruit for God's judgment on a people who gave him nothing (Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10-16, Micah 7:1), and they also performed acted prophecies: Jeremiah smashed a pot (Jeremiah 19) and wore a yoke (Jeremiah 27). William Telford (1980) showed how widely the fig tree served as a symbol of Israel and of blessing or judgment, and most modern commentators, including Morna Hooker and Joel Marcus, read the tree as an acted parable of the temple's fate. A tree in leaf at Passover could bear early unripe knobs, so its bare leaves were a show without substance, like a temple busy with worship and empty of the fruit God sought. John Chrysostom long ago noted that Jesus showed his power to judge on a tree, not on a person. As for the Jewish objection, many Christian scholars now reject the old reading outright: Mark aims the sign at the temple's leadership in a particular hour, not at the Jewish people, who in this chapter protect Jesus from those leaders (verse 18). Readers can grant that the story is strange and still see what Mark meant by it.

hard.q: Does Jesus promise that anything we ask for in prayer will be ours if we believe hard enough?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the objection comes from both believers and skeptics. Read plainly, verses 23 and 24 say that whoever does not doubt will have whatever he asks. Kenneth Hagin and the Word of Faith movement built a whole teaching on these verses: believers have what they say, and unanswered prayer shows a failure of faith. Skeptics take the same plain reading and test it. The Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer (published in the American Heart Journal, 2006), led by Herbert Benson, found that prayer by Christian groups for patients undergoing heart surgery had no effect on their recovery. If the promise means what it says, the skeptic argues, it is false; if it does not, why say it?

Most interpreters in every major tradition answer that the plain reading ignores the passage's frame. The saying begins with ‘Have faith in God’ (verse 22), directing trust to God rather than to the believer's own certainty, and it ends at once with the command to forgive (verse 25), which ties prayer to the heart and relationships of the one who prays. It was spoken on the road over the Mount of Olives in sight of the temple mount, and many commentators, including William Telford and N. T. Wright, think ‘this mountain’ points to that mountain: faith in God can see even the great religious center removed and need not fear its fall. Moving mountains was also a Jewish figure for doing what seems impossible (the Talmud calls a brilliant teacher an ‘uprooter of mountains’, b. Berakhot 64a). Elsewhere Jesus teaches his disciples to pray ‘your will be done’ (Matthew 6:10), and in Gethsemane he asks that the cup pass and submits when it does not (14:36). Paul asked three times to have his thorn removed and was refused (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). Christian writers from Augustine to Calvin taught that God answers prayer as a Father who knows what is good, not as a mechanism. On this reading the verses teach bold, expectant prayer that nothing is too hard for God, and they give no support to teaching that treats faith as a technique for controlling him. The skeptic's challenge remains a real one for the believer who prays, and the Gospel does not pretend otherwise: its central figure prayed and was crucified.

observe: Trace Mark's time markers through the chapter (verses 11, 12, 19, 20). What happens on each day?
What exactly does Jesus do in the temple (verses 15 to 17), and whom does his action affect?
What reasons do the leaders give among themselves for not answering Jesus' question (verses 31 and 32)?
interpret: How do the fig tree and the temple explain each other in Mark's arrangement of verses 12 to 21?
Why does Jesus answer the question about his authority by asking about John's baptism? What would the right answer about John imply about Jesus?
Why might Mark alone include the words ‘for all the nations’ in the quotation from Isaiah 56:7?
apply: The crowd welcomed Jesus with their own hopes for what his kingdom would be. What do you want Jesus to do for you that may not be what he came to do?
The fig tree had leaves and no fruit. Where might your own life or your church look healthy from a distance and give God little up close?
Jesus ties prayer to forgiveness. Is there someone you are holding something against, and what would releasing that debt to God look like?
